KA01.why: Both ask what a coefficient product means in a cost or interest model (1.08(18) there). Here the term 0.02x appears only after substituting into a two-account system and has to be read against an all-at-4% baseline. Different structure.
Both interpret a coefficient in a two-item money equation (12x + 15y = 600, read 0.8). GA02 reads a slope; KA01 reads a term made by substitution. Different asked quantity.
Generator flag. Both are two-variable money equations, but KA01 interprets a term made by substitution and KA13 converts a count variable into boxes. Different mechanism, so both are allowed.

KA02.why: Linear total cost with fixed cost plus a per-item cost, and average cost per item. Those items give the formula; here two (count, average) pairs are turned into totals and the slope is found. Different ask.
Both build a linear cost from two data points (here averages, in KA14 totals). Same building step, different asks.

KA03.why: Linear growth combined with a percent increase over an interval (f(12) is 12% more than f(10); find f(0)). Here no values are given, and the ask is the percent over a later, longer span.
Constant absolute growth compared with percent growth, and population percent increase. Different ask.

KA04.why: Both add the two equations to get at x + y. 002 has numeric coefficients and asks for x + y; here x + y is given, the coefficients are swapped symbolic constants, and a + b is asked.
Systems with constant coefficients and a structural ask. Different mechanism.

KA05.why: A ticket-revenue change caused by a price change, with a total ticket count, solved for the adult count. 327 swaps two given prices and gives the dollar difference. Here no prices are given and the revenue change is 0 (3a = 2c). Same family but a different mechanism.
The standard adult/child ticket system. Here no prices or total revenue are given.

KA06.why: A combined work rate for two pipes (together time given). That item leads to a quadratic; here a together time plus a sequential run give a linear system in the rates.
A pump at a constant rate. Single pump, trivial version.

KA07.why: A body-measurement formula where inputs change (BSA with height and mass +10%). That one is multiplicative and asks for a percent; here it is linear, with two opposite-sign changes and an absolute change asked.
Evaluating a two-input linear rule. Different ask.

KA08.why: A constant in an inequality is bounded by a point being or not being a solution. 328 is one-variable with one point; here a half-plane slope gets a two-sided range from one point in and one point out.

KA10.why: A linear diver-depth model. That one is about descent rate and depth; here pressure is linear with a nonzero intercept and the trap is proportional reasoning.

KA11.why: Linear vs. exponential growth. Here a percent of a fixed initial value gives a linear model; build-the-equation ask.
Loses 4% of the charge at the start of each hour, so exponential. That is the mirror image (percent of the current value). Different model.

KA12.why: Counting how many integer values satisfy a compound constraint, with an inclusive count. The staircase uses divisors; here a fixed-total two-item revenue becomes 300 <= 200 + 5L <= 360.
Counting ticket combinations at an exact total. Different constraint type.

KA13.why: Re-expressing a linear model under a change of variable or units. Here a count is regrouped into boxes in a standard-form budget.
Generator flag. Two-item money equation, different mechanism (see KA01).

KA14.why: Two pricing plans whose linear graphs are parallel (no common point). U01 asks for the condition on the constants; here plan B is built from two data points and the ask is a verbal comparison.
Comparing two cost plans. Different ask (meaning of a solution; break-even count).

KA15.why: Total time = travel time + fixed per-stop or loading time. Those give the formula. Here the travel time comes from a percent speed change (time scales by 1/1.2).

KC01.why: Means converted to totals, and a sub-group mean found by subtraction. 223 uses disjoint parts; here the windows overlap and the overlap is found by inclusion-exclusion.

Generator flag. Both turn means of day-windows into totals. KC01 finds an overlap of two fixed windows; KC11 finds the value that leaves a sliding window (change in total = in minus out). Different mechanism and ask, so both are allowed. Avoid placing them next to each other.

KC02.why: Mathematically the same as the equal-distance round-trip average speed (harmonic mean of 15 and 30 = 20, against 60/40 there), with the trap being the arithmetic mean of the two rates. These are ACT-bank items; no SAT item does it, so it is allowed. Note the reskin.
Round trip at 50/30 mph, but asks for a distance, not an average rate.

Generator flag. Both are weighted averages with the unweighted mean as the trap. KC02 weights by shares bought (equal dollars, harmonic); KC12 weights by days (arithmetic). Different mechanism, so both are allowed. Keep them apart.

KC03.why: Missing cell in a two-way table, found from an equality of two probabilities. 607 equates a row conditional with an overall marginal; here the two conditionals are reverses with the same numerator, so the row total equals the column total. Different key insight.
Missing cell from a given conditional, then the reverse conditional. Different ask.

KC04.why: Percent of a percent (forward) and whole from a percent. Here two successive losses are undone in reverse.
The same reverse successive-percent mechanism appears three times in this set (see within_list_cues).

KC05.why: The same two-level percent chain (percent of a percent) run forward. Here it runs backward from the count.

Same mechanism and same asked quantity: a base multiplied by a chain of successive fractions equals a given final count, so find the base (13,640 / (0.62 x 0.55) vs 1,512 / (0.7 x 0.75 x 0.8)). KC13 is the harder version with three steps; KC05 is redundant inside this set.

KC06.why: Same ask: profit as a percent of the selling price, and the same trap of using the cost as the base. The ACT item gives dollars ($40 cost, $50 price); here only a 60% markup is given. Cross-exam, so not a drop, but this is near-template.
Markup on cost, then a sale. 065 even uses a 60% markup. Different asks.

KC07.why: Same history numbers (mean 70, SD 8) and the first step is that item: how many SDs above the mean. Here the standing is then carried to a second distribution.
Two score distributions with means and SDs. Different ask.

KC08.why: Same core step: a given absolute change is p% of the original, so original = change / p (12 is 30% of the start, 40; here 150 is 25% of the original, 600). 421 adds a 'rate times days' step; KC08 adds a proportionality step. Thin, but not the same wrapper.
Scaling a recipe by proportion; output change from an input percent change. Different ask.

KC09.why: Dividing profit in a ratio. There the ratio is given; here it is built from amount times months.
Splitting a cost in proportion to a measure. Different weighting.

KC10.why: Same mechanism and same ask with the numbers changed: a 2x3 vs 2x2 two-way table of members/nonmembers, P(member OR column category) by inclusion-exclusion. The distractor set is identical in kind: 'and' (96/400 vs 40/250), members only (150/400 vs 100/250), key, and the double-counted sum (0.79 vs 0.88). BC04 was not drafted into batches 030-063, but it is an earlier idea and this re-uses it.
An OR probability with overlap (hearts or face cards).

KC11.why: A change in mean from replacing one value in a fixed-size set (change in total = new - old). 084 gives both values and asks for the new mean; here the change in mean and the new value are given and the removed value is asked. Inverse direction, same identity.
Value removed or added, from a change in mean. The set size changes there; here it stays at 7.

KC12.why: A weighted mean with the unweighted mean as the trap (time-weighted average speed; class means). Here the weights are days.

KC13.why: Whole from percents of one base; a chain of percents of different bases (forward). Here three successive remainders are reversed from a dollar amount.
Same reverse successive-percent chain (see KC05). Keep KC13 and drop KC05.

KC14.why: Same mechanism and ask: a line-of-best-fit slope applied to a change in x given in raw units when x is in scaled units ($1,000 = 10 hundreds; 300 kg = 3 hundreds), then the predicted change in y converted to the asked unit (thousands of dollars; per 100 km times 2.5). The distractors match one for one: forgets the x scale (C there / B here), stops before the y conversion (A there / C here). The extra trip-length step only changes the final unit factor.
Slope times a difference in x on a line of best fit. Asks for a difference in residuals.
Liters per 100 km contexts. Different mechanism.

KC15.why: Part-to-whole rate. No bank or idea item compares rates per 100,000.

within_list_cues.KC04 / KC05 / KC13: Three ideas in one set reverse a chain of successive percents (known final amount / product of retained fractions). KC05 is a template of KC13; KC04 differs only in context (two losses). Keep at most two; drop KC05.
within_list_cues.KC01 / KC11: Both convert window means to totals. They differ in mechanism (overlap by inclusion-exclusion vs. sliding-window in-minus-out), so both are allowed but should not be adjacent.
within_list_cues.KC02 / KC12: Both are weighted means with the unweighted mean of the rates as trap choice. KC02 is harmonic (equal dollars), KC12 is weighted by days. Both are allowed.
within_list_cues.KA01 / KA13: Both are two-variable money equations. KA01 interprets a substituted term; KA13 regroups a variable into boxes. Both are allowed.
within_list_cues.KA02 / KA14: Both build a linear cost from two data points (averages to totals in KA02; totals in KA14). Different asks.
within_list_cues.KC03 / KC10: Two two-way-table probability items in one set (missing cell from reverse conditionals; union). Different asks.
within_list_cues.KA03: SPR. The key falls out by letting the 2010 population be 100 (25, then 125, then 175, so 50/125). That is a legitimate SAT strategy, not a defect; the item still tests base-shift reasoning.
within_list_cues.KC04: Mild cue: the key, 7.50, is the largest choice, and a student who knows the raw weight must be 'divided by both losses' can pick the largest without computing. Consider adding the subtract-both-percents distractor 4.5/0.55 = 8.18 so the key is not the extreme.
within_list_cues.KA08: Not a cue: every choice must be checked against both points, as the generator says. Testing either point alone eliminates only one or two choices.
within_list_cues.KC08: Choice B's rationale (150/0.8 = 187.5) is weak; no natural misconception produces it. Consider 750 (150 x 5, which treats 150 as 1/5 of the new amount) or 450 alone.
within_list_cues.other: No choice gives the answer away in KA01, KA07, KA09-KA14, KC06, KC07, KC09, KC10, KC12, KC14 or KC15, and no second defensible answer was found. In KA01, the equivalent phrasing 'extra interest from investing x at 6% rather than 4%' is not offered as a separate choice, so A is unique.
